title: Mitigating Over-squashing without Rewiring: A Sheaf Effective Resistance Perspective
claim: Baselines lose accuracy as the required propagation distance grows; only our method keeps perfect accuracy at every distance.
layout: single line plot, accuracy vs problem radius, value labels at points
description: A single line chart with a dotted grid. The x-axis is the problem radius r, from 2 to 8, and the y-axis is accuracy from 0 to 1. Seven colored lines with distinct markers are listed in a legend at the lower left: FlatNSD-SAGE (black pentagon), FlatNSD-MLP (orange asterisk), BuNN (cyan plus), GGNN (green square), GAT (blue circle), GIN (purple diamond) and GCN (red triangle). The black FlatNSD-SAGE line stays flat at 1.0 along the top for every r. The baselines start at 1.0 and fall at different radii. GCN, GIN and GAT drop at r=4. GGNN drops at r=5. FlatNSD-MLP drops sharply at r=6. BuNN holds until r=6 and then falls to 0.71 and 0.42. Numeric labels sit next to the markers. The eye goes first to the flat top line and then to the steep falling curves.
caption: Training accuracy for the TreeNeighborsMatch task. Results for GCN, GIN, GAT, and GGNN are from [ref]. Results for BuNN are from [ref]. Only FlatNSD-SAGE achieves perfect accuracy for all $r$. \looseness=-1
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to over-squashing -- a phenomenon in which the repeated compression of node embeddings into finite-size messages causes representations to collapse. Over-squashing is most often diagnosed as a property of the graph topology, with effective resistance serving as a principled measure of the bottleneck. We provide a complementary view on the matter: building on cellular sheaves, we introduce sheaf effective resistance, a generalization of effective resistance that depends on the sheaf attached to the graph, and we prove that for flat vector bundles, the over-squashing sensitivity in the Jacobian sense is upper bounded by a quantity related to the sheaf effective resistance between the nodes. The bottleneck thus need not lie in the graph itself: it can be relocated, and reduced, by adjusting the sheaf. We instantiate this idea in FlatNSD, a simple message-passing variant of Neural Sheaf Diffusion, and show that it implicitly learns to modulate total sheaf effective resistance, performing well on benchmarks designed to stress over-squashing without altering the original graph topology.
